comment: Diagram fixtures for node/edge recovery (xberg-io/xberg#579). Each entry says what the
fixture is, where it came from, why it is in the set, and what the correct answer is.
`class` is the recovery mode the fixture measures, and it decides how it should be scored:
A -- the file states its graph outright (connector endpoints, model ids, source/target
attributes, or diagram source text). Recovery is lossless, so a correct
implementation scores exactly 1.0. Anything less is a bug, not a tuning problem.
B -- the file carries geometry only. The graph has to be inferred from shapes, strokes
and text positions, so scoring is precision/recall against a threshold.
`states_graph_in_metadata` marks a Class-B file that also happens to name its own graph.
Every producer does it somewhere, and rarely only once: Graphviz writes one <title> per node
holding the node id and one per edge holding `src->dst`, and repeats both in XML comments;
Mermaid names both endpoints in `id="L_start_auth_0"`, again in `data-id`, and gives the
edge's waypoints outright in `data-points` as base64 JSON; PlantUML names them in
`id="Read config-to-Open input"`, again in a comment, again as a `data-entity-1`/
`data-entity-2` adjacency pair, and then embeds its entire deflated source in a
`<?plantuml-src?>` processing instruction -- which is why a file can look clean in plain
text and still hand over the whole answer to anyone who decodes it. Such a
file cannot measure geometry recovery, because a recogniser can score perfectly without
reading a single coordinate -- and xberg's SVG extractor already reads <title>. Those
fixtures therefore ship twice, and `geometry_only_variant` names the second copy, produced
by `scripts/strip_svg_graph_metadata.py`. The two share one ground truth: same answer,
arrived at a harder way. Reading the metadata when it is there is correct behaviour -- it
is just a different capability, and the two are measured apart.
Ground truth is keyed by node label, so an unlabelled decoration -- PlantUML's start and
stop markers, an arrowhead, a leader dot -- has no key and is not a node. Cluster, swimlane
and lane containers are not nodes either, however closed their outlines look.
The PDF fixtures under `diagrams/pdf/` need no `geometry_only_variant`, and the reason is
worth stating: the container strips the metadata by itself. A PDF page holds path operators
and positioned glyphs and nothing else -- no element ids, no <title>, no class attribute --
so every one of them is geometry-only by construction. They are the strictest Class-B
measurement in the set, and the ones that share a ground truth with an SVG fixture separate
what an implementation knows about graphs from what it knows about SVG.
Every PDF is written by its producer and then rebuilt with `qpdf --empty --deterministic-id
--pages <raw> 1-z --`, which drops the `Info` dictionary the producer stamps the clock into
and derives the file id from the content. Without that no two runs of the same command agree
byte for byte. `scripts/build_diagram_pdfs.py` runs both halves, and its `--check` mode
rebuilds and compares, so `producer.command` stays a claim that can be tested rather than a
note about what someone once ran. PDFs embed subsetted fonts, so that check is machine-local;
reproducing across machines is what `corpus.lock.json` is for.
A PDF embeds subsetted outlines of whatever fonts the renderer reached for, and this corpus is
public, so the embedding permission of those fonts is ours to check. Every family in the set was
verified through the OS/2 fsType bit of the system font it came from, and
`scripts/build_diagram_pdfs.py` fails a build that reaches for anything not on that allowlist.
It is why there is no CJK PDF: macOS's Songti reports fsType 2, restricted, which forbids
embedding without the owner's permission, so `graphviz_cjk` ships as SVG only until an
open-licensed CJK face is available to render it.
`page` is 1-based. `bbox` is [x0, y0, x1, y1] in the container's own units -- SVG user space,
or points from the top-left of the PDF page -- measured across the graph's node outlines. Both
run y downwards; PDF user space runs y upwards, so a consumer reading raw PDF coordinates has
to flip. It is recorded only where the page holds more than the graph, because that is the
only time it distinguishes an answer that is right from one that is right by accident.

fixtures.notes: dir=back draws the arrowhead at the tail, so the ground truth records the drawn direction, not the declaration order.
The two cluster rectangles are containers, not nodes. Reporting either is a false positive, and the stripped variant removes the <title> that would have given the game away.
Two edges cross in the middle of the drawing and share no endpoint at either end. A recogniser that joins strokes where they intersect invents a node there, an edge, or both.
Orthogonal elbow routing is the default in every non-Graphviz diagram tool, and an elbow leg can run alongside an unrelated node before turning.

One record is one node drawn as a single outline divided by internal rules, and edges terminate on a named port rather than the shape. Splitting a record into one node per field is the failure this looks for, so the node key is the field texts as one multi-line label.
No node in this drawing has a fill, so a recogniser keying on filled regions finds nothing. Labels are Japanese, Korean, Hebrew and Arabic.

128 nodes and 141 edges, for the perf and memory profiling the review on xberg#1410 asked for. Regenerable from one rule: a complete binary tree over N0..N127 plus a dashed shortcut N_i -> N_i+16 for every i divisible by 8.

Mermaid's idioms are nothing like Graphviz's: a 4.4 KB CSS <style> block, ten <marker> defs, HTML labels in a <foreignObject>, and every edge label drawn on an opaque background rect (class="labelBkg") that looks exactly like a small node. It names both endpoints of every edge in id="L_start_auth_0", repeats it in data-id, and gives that edge's exact waypoint list a third time in data-points as base64 JSON.

PlantUML states each edge four times over: id="Read config-to-Open input", an XML comment <!--link Read config to Open input-->, a data-entity-1/data-entity-2 pair that is an adjacency list in its own right, and a <?plantuml-src?> processing instruction carrying the entire deflated source. The (*) start and end are unlabelled markers, so they are not nodes and the two edges joining them are not edges. PlantUML itself is GPL; its SVG output is not a derivative of it.

Swimlanes: three labelled bands spanning the drawing, each holding activities that belong to it. A band is not a node. This file states nothing in plain text -- no id, no class, no comment -- but it carries a <?plantuml-src?> processing instruction whose payload is the whole .puml source, raw-deflated and 6-bit encoded, comments and all. Decoding it hands over every node, every edge, and the lane each activity sits in, so the stripped variant is what measures anything here.

This was long held up as the one dialect that states nothing, on the grounds that its classes give a shape's type (com.sun.star.drawing.ConnectorShape) without naming what it connects. That was wrong, and the counting shows it: the file carries exactly 4 <g class="...CustomShape"> and 3 <g class="...ConnectorShape">, against a ground truth of exactly 4 nodes and 3 edges. Type per element, applied to every element, is the node/edge partition -- which is most of the answer, however little any one class says on its own. It ships with a stripped variant now. What remains genuinely hard is that glued connectors start and end a few units short of the shape outline, so endpoints match only by proximity.

The same drawing as an ODF source, and the first Class A fixture in the corpus. Every draw:connector names its endpoints outright with draw:start-shape and draw:end-shape against the draw:id of a shape, so recovery is a lookup and must be exact. Rendering this file is what produced diagrams/svg/libreoffice_connectors.svg, so one ground truth covers both the stated graph and the inferred one.

Every shape and label sits under a chain of transform attributes, and the viewBox is half the viewport, so nothing lands at the coordinate it is written at. A recogniser that reads coordinates literally puts every label outside its box.

The AWS/Azure architecture house style: a node is an icon glyph with its caption underneath and no bounding outline at all, so every label sits outside every closed region and no node has a border to find.

The same outline-free icon house style as icon_nodes.svg, but each glyph is drawn as several separate sibling elements that overlap rather than as one path with several subpaths, so the recovered node extent has to be the union of its parts. A recogniser that treats every element as its own candidate returns eight nodes; one that keeps only the largest element per glyph loses the cap. Every glyph is topped by a part that reaches above the body, and Archive's ellipse is wider than the path beneath it, so neither part's box is the union in either axis on its own.

Every other fixture is entirely a diagram or entirely not one. This page is both: a heading, two paragraphs, a four-row ruled table, and one figure at the foot. Recovery has to be selective within the page rather than deciding once per file, and the table must contribute nothing. The table's task column reads Compile/Approval/Release, chosen to share no label with the figure's Build/Sign-off/Ship, so returning the table's cells as nodes scores zero instead of scoring full marks by accident. bbox is the figure's extent in the SVG user space.

Two graphs on one page, sharing no node and no edge. `ground_truth/dot/<stem>.dot` cannot express that, so this is the fixture that makes the manifest's `graphs` array carry its weight: the two answers live in `<stem>.g0.dot` and `<stem>.g1.dot` and it is the manifest, not the file layout, that says so. Nothing in the markup separates the figures -- only whitespace and a caption do -- so a recogniser has to segment the page rather than return one graph of seven nodes.

The same graph as diagrams/svg/graphviz_flow.svg, drawn by the same layout engine into a different container. Scoring the pair apart separates what the recogniser knows about graphs from what it knows about SVG.

Orthogonal routing as PDF path operators. An elbow that was one <path> with an explicit `d` in SVG arrives here as a run of `m`/`l` operators with no element boundary around them, so the segments of one edge have to be rejoined from geometry alone.

128 nodes and 141 edges, for the throughput and memory profiling the review on xberg#1410 asked for. The PDF copy matters separately from the SVG one because the cost of recovery here is dominated by content-stream parsing, not by graph size.
Two graphs on one PDF page. Both bboxes are in points from the top-left of the page.

Mermaid's drawing through Skia rather than cairo, and the one producer whose SVG cannot be converted by librsvg at all: mermaid puts every label in a <foreignObject> of HTML, which librsvg does not render, so a cairo copy of this file would have no text in it. It is also the fixture that scored zero nodes and zero edges against the SVG implementation, so the PDF copy says whether that was the dialect or the geometry.

Prose, a ruled table and one figure on a single PDF page -- the container where xberg already runs table detection, so the two have to coexist rather than one winning. bbox is the figure's extent in points from the top-left of the page.

Four printed pages with the diagram on page 3: page 1 and page 4 are prose, page 2 is a ruled table. This is the fixture the page-reference half of xberg#579 needs, and the only one where an answer can be right about the graph and wrong about where it is. Pages 1, 2 and 4 must yield nothing.

The third PDF writer, and the drawing that spans both classes: the .fodg source names each connector's endpoints outright and scores exactly 1.0, this PDF keeps only the strokes. Same graph, same layout, one container that answers the question and one that does not.

Nine boxes and only three edges, so six nodes are isolated -- a recogniser that reports only the connected component silently loses two thirds of the graph. Each box carries a name and a role on separate lines, which is one node with a two-line label rather than two nodes.

fixtures.reason: A table drawn as ruling lines has the same signature as a diagram: closed rectangular regions with text inside them, joined by straight strokes running from the edge of one region to the next. This is the most dangerous negative in the set, because whatever rejects it also has to not break table detection.

Each label sits in its own rounded box joined to its slice by a two-segment leader line ending in a dot, which is exactly the shape of a labelled node wired up by an elbow connector. The leader lines connect nothing and the slices are not nodes.

A printed form: captions beside empty boxes, section rules, a row of checkboxes, a signature line. Every ingredient of a diagram is present and there is no graph, and the rules in particular run right up to the boxes, which is what an edge looks like.

The ruled table in the container where it does the most damage. A PDF table is drawn as ruling strokes and positioned glyphs with nothing to say it is a table, which is the same evidence a connector-and-box recogniser reads. Whatever rejects this must also leave xberg's existing PDF table detection intact.
The pie chart that the SVG implementation already reports as a five-node, four-edge graph. Carried into PDF so the false positive can be measured in both containers rather than argued about in one.
bar chart: closed outlines and straight strokes, but the strokes are axes and gridlines, not connectors
two unconnected shapes and one label; there is no graph to recover

Despite the filename this is an inferno flame graph, not a paging diagram: 77 nested <rect> elements, 81 <text> labels, 76 <g> wrappers, a CSS <style> block, an ECMAScript <script>, and a gradient <defs>. Adjacency here is stack containment, not connection, and there is not one connector in the file. It is the hardest negative in the corpus and it was already shipping -- the only thing missing was the assertion that recovery returns nothing.
